analysis.one_liner: Caps speculative positions in commodity derivatives markets and forces public reporting of who is trading what.
analysis.headline: The House Agriculture Committee approved the bill by voice vote in December 2009, but it never received a House floor vote and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 financial crisis, this bill targeted the largely unregulated market in commodity derivatives — the financial contracts tied to oil, food, and other physical goods. It would have required the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to set limits on how big a speculative bet any one trader can hold, publish monthly data showing how much of the market is pure speculation versus real hedging, and close a loophole that let traders reach U.S. markets through foreign exchanges with looser rules. It also would have required most derivatives to be settled through regulated clearinghouses and given the CFTC emergency power to suspend trading in credit default swaps, the instruments at the center of the AIG bailout.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers of food, gasoline, and other commodities, who bear the cost when speculation pushes prices beyond what supply and demand justify. Farmers, airlines, and other genuine hedgers also benefit from rules that reserve market liquidity for actual commercial users and from public data that exposes manipulation. Taxpayers benefit indirectly from reduced systemic risk in the derivatives market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of fuel, food, and energy

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CFTC to set hard position limits on speculative holdings in futures and options on physical commodities, aimed at preventing excessive speculation, manipulation, squeezes, and corners [S2] [S3].

Directs the CFTC to publish monthly, disaggregated data on index-fund and other passive positions and on speculative positions relative to bona fide hedgers, so the public can see who is driving prices [S2] [S3].

Bars U.S.-located participants from accessing foreign exchanges that trade contracts settling against U.S. prices unless those exchanges publish comparable daily data and adopt comparable position limits, closing an offshore regulatory loophole [S2] [S3].

Makes regulatory exemptions available only for derivatives settled and cleared through registered clearing organizations, and lets the CFTC summarily suspend credit default swap trading when investor protection requires it and prosecute criminal violations if the Justice Department declines [S2] [S3].

Treats greenhouse-gas emission allowances and offset credits as regulated commodities and prepares CFTC oversight to prevent speculation in a future carbon market, and adds CFTC enforcement staff [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large derivatives dealers, hedge funds, and other big speculators, who would face position limits, detailed reporting of their positions, and clearing requirements; foreign exchanges that would have to match U.S. transparency rules to keep U.S. customers. End users who hedge could face somewhat higher compliance and clearing costs, and stricter limits could slightly reduce market liquidity.

drawbacks.text: Position limits can reduce market liquidity, and the bill acknowledges this trade-off by requiring the CFTC to set limits in a way that preserves liquidity for bona fide hedgers, with public hearings taking input from commercial hedgers before limits are set [S3].

The mandatory clearing requirement routes over-the-counter trades through registered clearinghouses (with a waiver only for highly customized, infrequently traded deals), imposing new clearing costs and concentrating counterparty risk in a smaller set of clearing institutions [S3].

Critics of commodity position limits generally argue speculators provide liquidity and that limits raise hedging costs for end users; the bill's own study of over-the-counter position limits concedes the consequences needed to be tested before extending limits to exempt markets [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real, documented problem after 2008: an opaque over-the-counter derivatives market with few position limits, which contributed to both commodity price volatility and systemic risk. The main costs — clearing fees for end users and somewhat reduced speculative liquidity — are modest compared with the transparency and stability gains, and the bill built in hedger input and waiver authority to blunt them. One caveat: by the time it died, Congress was already writing broader derivatives rules elsewhere, so this bill's practical significance was partly as a blueprint. Its clearing mandate and position-limit framework closely resemble provisions that later became law in the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act, which suggests the substance was not the obstacle.

outcome.mechanism: The House Agriculture Committee approved it by voice vote and it was printed for the full House, but no floor vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Collin Peterson, chairman of the House Agriculture Committee, introduced the bill on February 11, 2009, and it was referred to the Agriculture and Financial Services Committees [S1] [S5].
The Agriculture Committee marked it up the very next day and ordered it reported amended by voice vote, though it was not formally reported until December 19, 2009 [S5].

On December 19, 2009, the Financial Services and Judiciary Committees were discharged and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 223 — the last step before House floor consideration [S3] [S5].
No floor action was ever taken; the bill sat on the calendar until the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large over-the-counter derivatives dealers and foreign exchanges avoided this bill's position limits, reporting mandates, and clearing requirements. In practice the policy fight moved to a broader financial overhaul, and similar derivatives rules were enacted the following year in the Dodd-Frank Act, so much of the substance was not lost — but this bill itself never became law.

for.name: Collin C. Peterson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, steered it through the Agriculture Committee, and secured its amendment and voice-vote report in February 2009

for.name: House Agriculture Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill one day after introduction, ordered it reported amended by voice vote, and reported it with H. Rept. 111-385 in December 2009

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote after it reached the Union Calendar; the House instead handled derivatives regulation within a broader financial overhaul bill

against.name: Over-the-counter derivatives dealers and exchanges
against.role: Banks, hedge funds, and futures exchanges active in OTC and offshore markets
against.what_they_did: Opposed position limits and clearing mandates on derivatives trading through lobbying during the 2009-10 financial regulation debate

sides.party_line_note: The record contains no roll-call votes, so the partisan split cannot be measured; every sponsor and all 25 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no recorded opposition ever appeared in the action history.

industries.industry: Over-the-counter derivatives dealers and large speculators (major banks, hedge funds, energy traders)
industries.note: The bill imposes position limits, special-call access to their books and records, detailed reporting, and possible suspension of credit default swap trading. Their profit depends on large, opaque positions in markets that set prices for food and fuel, so their interest runs against the transparency the bill imposes.

The bill makes regulatory exemptions available only for trades settled and cleared through registered clearing organizations, routing the over-the-counter market through them and making them the permanent gatekeepers of derivatives settlement. It also adds disclosure, daily publication, and fitness requirements for them.

Exchanges outside the U.S. would lose direct U.S. access for contracts settling against U.S. prices unless they publish comparable daily data and adopt comparable position limits. This targets the practice of moving trades offshore to escape U.S. oversight.

The bill defines greenhouse-gas emission allowances and offset credits as regulated commodities and directs CFTC coordination with Agriculture for a market-based greenhouse gas program, giving a future carbon trading market a regulated framework designed to prevent speculation.
